newsitem.title: USA: Cadillac drops Cindy Crawford, the duck stays.
newsitem.headline: Cadillac drops Cindy Crawford, the duck stays.

text.p: Cindy is out. The duck stays.

That's the news from Cadillac, General Motors Corp.'s luxury car division Thursday. Officials confirmed they have dropped television advertisements that reveal nearly as much of supermodel Cindy Crawford as the new Catera car after objections from female employees at the automaker.
"We've pulled it for the time being from our national schedules so we can study it more," said Cadillac spokesman James Williams.

In the ad, Crawford, wearing a short skirt and knee-high boots, plays a bored princess looking for excitment. She finds it in the form of the Catera. Helping her is a bouncy red duck, which the division is using to demonstrate the Catera is a "new kind" of Cadillac.
Cadillac desperately needs to attract younger buyers, and the Catera, introduced last November, is supposed to do just that by appealing to affluent Baby Boomers who would otherwise buy an import.

Cadillac also hopes half of Catera buyers will be women. So how does the comely Crawford help that? Tom Wilkinson, who heads up public relations for Catera, said Cadillac needed an eye-catching theme to stand out among the other Super Bowl ads, which is where the ad first ran.

"The intention was to do an ad that was high camp," he said. "It just didn't work out as well as we hoped it would. There were a few GM executives who were uncomforable with the ad and felt it was sexist."

He adds that, because of the time constraints of the Super Bowl, the spot was not tested as extensively as it might have otherwise been. In addition, the original celebrity Cadillac wanted, singer Barry White, had to back out.

All told, Cadillac spent at least $2 million on the spot, said Jean Halliday, Detroit bureau chief for Advertising Age, an industry trade publication. She questioned GM's thinking given its brand management strategy of targeting advertisements for specific customer segments.

"It shouldn't take a genius to figure out that Cindy Crawford in high leather boots and a short skirt wouldn't appeal to educated professional women," she said. "I think it's just another example of how male-dominated the auto industry is. It took female GM executives after the ad was running for a month to convince Cadillac to pull it."

Cadillac officials said that, of the approximately 4,300 Cateras sold since the car was introduced, about half the buyers were women and buyers overall are mainly in their 40s and 50s, on track with internal projections.

What of the duck? Wilkinson said the fowl's future is safe, although its use will evolve through later Catera ads. Dealers, meantime, say they would like to see less of the duck and more of the car in advertisements.
"We're not selling ducks. We're selling cars," said Bill Collins, sales manager of Don Massey Cadillac Inc. in Plymouth, Mich., which bills itself as the world's largest Cadillac dealer.
Added Collins, "I think they made a mistake. They probably should have kept Cindy and gotten rid of the duck."
